conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes 'yes', stating that randomized trials demonstrate low-dose CT screening reduces lung cancer mortality among heavy current or recent ex-smokers.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: yes—among people at high risk from substantial current or recent past smoking, randomized trials show that low-dose CT screening reduces deaths from lung cancer.** This is a mortality benefit, not merely earlier diagnosis.

In the US National Lung Screening Trial (53,454 high-risk participants), three annual low-dose CT screens were compared with chest radiography. Lung-cancer mortality was 20% lower with CT (relative risk 0.80; 95% CI 0.73–0.93). The comparison matters: CT was better than chest X-ray, not proof that any CT frequency benefits every former smoker.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21714641/

The independent Dutch–Belgian NELSON randomized trial compared volume low-dose CT screening with no screening in high-risk current and former smokers. It likewise found significantly lower lung-cancer mortality; reported 10-year reductions were about 24% in men and 33% in women (the estimate in women was less precise because fewer women enrolled).  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793

Thus, your answer is supported for the populations studied—typically heavy smokers who currently smoke or quit relatively recently—not necessarily for all “ex-smokers,” especially those who quit long ago or have lower cumulative exposure. In the US, the USPSTF recommends **annual** low-dose CT for adults aged 50–80 with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years, with stopping when a person has quit for 15 years or cannot/would not undergo curative treatment.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening

Screening also has harms: false-positive findings, follow-up imaging or invasive procedures, incidental findings, radiation, and possible overdiagnosis. The benefit therefore depends on eligibility, reliable repeat screening, high-quality follow-up, and shared decision-making—not CT alone. A Cochrane review synthesized eight mortality trials (91,122 participants), supporting evaluation of both benefits and harms.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD013829.pub2/full
